Just like on social media, you can like your favourite moments and share them with friends and family in your group chats. There's no limit to the moments you can watch - just swipe through and find fresh videos every time you come to the feed.

You're one tap away from live scores in the Sky Sports app - and by following your favourites, you'll see the scores that matter to you right at the top of your screen.

You can also filter push notifications to stay up-to-date with the latest breaking news from your favourite sports, as well as heading straight to the Sky Sports Transfer Centre for all the latest moves and gossip.

A reminder... it's free! But make sure you're signed in for the best experience.

Yes, the Sky Sports app supports a built-in dark mode. It automatically matches your phone's system settings or can be toggled manually inside the app's display or appearance preferences.

articles.title: Totti se abre: "Para hacer las paces con Spalletti, tendríamos que decirnos toda la verdad"
articles.standfirst: Francesco Totti habla en su autobiografía sobre su acercamiento con el técnico Spalleti tras su tormentosa relación
articles.summary: Francesco Totti habla en su autobiografía sobre su acercamiento con el técnico Spalleti tras su tormentosa relación
articles.body: El diario italiano 'La Gazzetta dello Sport' publica fragmentos del libro 'Oltre' (Más allá de), la autobiografía de Francesco Totti publicada por 'Cairo Editore'. El mítico capitán de la Roma relata su tormentosa relación con el entrenador Luciano Spalletti, con el que coincidió cinco año y medio en el equipo romano, y confiesa que estuvo cerca de volver a jugar al fútbol con 48 años. "Dije que no a la Serie A. Dije que no al Génova. Dije que no al Como. Tenía 48 años. El entrenador del Génova era Alberto Gilardino, campeón del mundo como yo con Italia en 2006, mientras que en el banquillo del Como ya estaba Cesc Fàbregas, uno de los grandes de la historia del fútbol... Gilardino tenía 42 años, Fàbregas 37, así que habría tenido respectivamente 6 y 11 años más que quienes cobraban por decirme qué hacer. No son leyendas urbanas, es la pura verdad. Increíble, pero cierta. Una locura", compartió. Totti comenta en el libro que "tenía 48 años, de acuerdo, pero la edad de alguna manera se puede superar; uno se vuelve más lento, pero el pie no envejece. Todos de acuerdo: ese no necesita bótox. La Roma era el punto. No el problema, nunca lo será. Una traición deportiva no tiene edad, ya tengas 18 ó 48 años". "Para hacer las paces de verdad con Luciano Spalletti, tendríamos que decirnos toda la verdad", destacó el exfutbolista de 49 años. Totti explicó que "las condiciones para la paz entre Luciano Spalletti y yo se van perfilando día a día. Digamos que hemos emprendido un camino que va más allá del silencio que existía entre nosotros. No voy a repetir aquí el origen de nuestro distanciamiento; esa historia la conocen hasta los marcianos. Lo interesante es lo que sucedió después". "Desde el 28 de mayo de 2017 —el día de mi retiro forzoso— y durante más de seis años, no nos vimos ni nos hablamos. Ninguno sintió la necesidad del otro. Seguimos caminos separados. Luego, en noviembre de 2023, las cosas empezaron a cambiar. Vito Scala, mi amigo de toda la vida, me llamó. 'Oye, ¿sabes que Italia juega contra Macedonia en Roma el día 17, verdad?'. 'Sí, ¿y qué?'. 'Una delegación de la selección nacional va a visitar el Bambino Gesù'. Es decir, el hospital infantil al que suelo acudir de vez en cuando —sin decírselo a nadie— para saludar a los jóvenes pacientes. 'Me parece muy bien'. 'Pues, mira, deberías ir tú también'. '¿Por qué, Vito?'. 'Porque será un momento estupendo. Estarán el presidente de la federación, Gabriele Gravina; tu amigo Gigi Buffon, Giovanni Di Lorenzo; también vendrá Angelo Peruzzi. Y...'. '¿Y?'. 'Y el seleccionador nacional'. Es decir, Luciano Spalletti. 'No'. No quería saber nada del asunto. 'Vamos, piénsalo...'". Francesco Totti relató que "lo pensé bien, y me di cuenta de que está bien ser egoísta —protegerse del dolor y ocultar las heridas—, pero no a costa de los demás. 'Vito, vale'. Haces la vista gorda y escuchas a tu corazón. Intentas dejar el pasado atrás por una causa noble. Así que acepté la invitación; al fin y al cabo, tarde o temprano tenía que ocurrir. El mundo del fútbol es pequeño. O le saludaba o le daba un cabezazo. Aquel día llegué antes que él. En mi scooter. Entré en el vestíbulo. En medio del ajetreo, Vito se puso serio: 'Ya están llegando'. Yo llevaba una chaqueta de cuero; él, un traje oscuro. El presidente Gravina hizo gala de su encanto: 'Este es Luciano Spalletti…'. Quien, debo decir, dijo las palabras adecuadas para romper la tensión: 'Por el lado del corazón... ¿te doy un abrazo? Por el lado del corazón, entonces...'. Un choque de manos rápido. Un abrazo. Fue un gesto fugaz, nada más. No sentí nada; todavía no era amor. Ni un vuelco, ni un escalofrío: absolutamente nada. Volví a verle en el Olímpico de Roma el 14 de mayo de 2025, en la final de la Coppa Italia que el Bolonia ganó al Milan. '¿Cómo va todo?'. 'Todo bien, ¿y tú?'. 'Bien, gracias'. 'Adiós'. 'Adiós'. Las cortesías de siempre, sin ninguna emoción real. Luego, cada uno siguió su camino".

articles.title: Rankings aside, Jamil plans to catch Panama by surprise
articles.summary: Bengaluru: Khalid Jamil does not follow everything that is said about him on social media, but he has a pretty good idea how fans have reacted to some
articles.body: Bengaluru: Khalid Jamil does not follow everything that is said about him on social media, but he has a pretty good idea how fans have reacted to some recent performances of the national team.India’s failure to qualify for the AFC Asian Cup, the big blank at Unity Cup, lack of wins in Tajikistan have invited criticism from fans and pundits. The India coach knows brickbats are part of the job; he doesn’t mind, but some, he feels, have hit below the belt.“As long as the criticism is constructive, I am fine with it,” Jamil told TOI in a recent video call. “People with knowledge about football know what’s happening with the national team, why we have not been able to put together a string of wins. I don’t like when people criticise for the sake of it.”Jamil will be under the lens again as India play three friendlies during this FIFA international window, starting with Panama at the Sree Kanteerava Stadium here on Friday.Central America’s lone participants at the FIFA World Cup 2026 are the lowest-ranked opponent at 44, paling in comparison to five-time world champions Brazil and heavyweights Uruguay. There are, however, almost 100 places separating the two teams, yet the former India midfielder believes his side can catch the visitors by surprise.“Panama is a very good team, no doubt about that, but we cannot forget that we are playing at home. We must believe in ourselves and play attacking football. What happens on the field will dictate our gameplan, but I am positive. The crowd will be a big factor. They will be our 12th man, pushing us to secure a good result,” said Jamil.Panama have arrived here in batches from a dozen-odd countries. At Wednesday’s evening training session, there were 18 players on the field; five were said to have missed their flights and will join on Thursday, while three, including Norwich City defender Jose Cordoba, pulled out due to injuries.Coach Thomas Christiansen opted not to call up replacements for the three missing players.The last time India played at Sree Kanteerava, the crowd helped the national team punch above its weight and win the SAFF Championship 2023. There were back-to-back wins against strong Lebanon and Kuwait sides. This time around, all that the West Block Blues, Bengaluru FC’s vociferous fan club, promised was “an empty stadium” due to higher prices, not in tune with the comparatively lower profile of the opponents.According to sources, less than 6,000 tickets have been sold so far.Ticket sales typically pick up on the eve of the match. articles.title: Texas RB Hollywood Smothers surprisingly added to injury report, questionable vs. Tennessee
articles.summary: Smothers scored the game-winning touchdown against Ohio State two weeks ago.
articles.body:
The first injury report for this weekend's clash between No. 1 Texas and No. 14 Tennessee came with a bit of a surprise.

Texas starting running back Hollywood Smothers has been ruled questionable for the game, in addition to defensive lineman Justus Terry , defensive back Xavier Filsaime and offensive lineman Jordan Coleman all being ruled out. Tight end Nick Townsend is also doubtful.

Per On3 , Smothers is dealing with a lower body injury and his availability will be decided based on how the week progresses.

Smothers joined Steve Sarkisian's program this season after two years at North Carolina State. He's had a successful start with the Longhorns, logging 198 rushing yards on 41 carries, 54 receiving yards and three total touchdowns in three games for the undefeated team.

That included the game-winning leap in Texas' epic comeback win against then-No. 1 Ohio State .

If Smothers is unable to play, Raleek Brown has posted the second-most carries on the team with 31, which he has turned into 129 rushing yards and two touchdowns. Freshmen Derrek Cooper and Michael Terry III are the only other runners on the team with double-digit carries.

articles.title: Top 6 Bowl projections for BYU football ahead of Week 4
articles.summary: National analysts predict a historic College Football Playoff run for the Cougars, forecasting matchups against powerhouses like Alabama and Ohio State as Bi...
articles.body:
The BYU Cougars are entering Big 12 conference play after the bye week. But it's not too soon to look at bowl game projections. Six outlets with five different opponents, all in the College Football Playoff.

It's hard to believe all the majors agree BYU will be among the final 12 teams this season. After being skipped over each of the past two seasons, Kalani Sitake's team is ready to take the next step and definitely have to roster to make a deep run. Here's a look at the latest projections for the BYU football program.

This would be an interesting matchup on many levels. BYU to Tuscaloosa or Alabama to Provo? ESPN analysts are torn on how it will go down, but they have the Tide and Cougars meeting to start the postseason. Kyle Bonagura has BYU as the 9-seed playing at Alabama, while Mark Schlabach has the inverse with BYU hosting during the first round. The Tide haven't carried the same amount of hype since Nick Saban stepped down and Kalen DeBoer took over.

Nevertheless, Alabama is still a dangerous team with many weapons. This would be a great head-to-head quarterback matchup with Keelon Russell and Bear Bachmeier . Both passers have been camp counselors at the Manning Passing Academy in the past.

This one would be epic for BYU if they could pull off an upset at the Horseshoe. The preseason No. 1 team in the land would host the 10th-seeded Cougars under this scenario. Kalani Sitake going up against Ryan Day would be great to watch. BYU's secondary would be across the line from OSU WR Jeremiah Smith , who will be the next great receiver in the NFL.

Penn State in the Playoff during Matt Campbell's first season? USA TODAY Sports might be reaching here. However, the storyline is set up greatly for BYU. Kalani Sitake rejects Penn State in the offseason, but later faces the team in the postseason. The outlet has the Cougars beating the Nittany Lions in the first round. This would lead to Sitake being viewed as a hero who stayed to put BYU football on the map.

What's even more interesting is that USA TODAY has BYU advancing to play Notre Dame in the quarterfinals. A trilogy series all within a year? That would be outstanding football.

Are people still on the "Lane train" after LSU's loss to Ole Miss? We'll see how the Tigers bounce back this season. According to SI, LSU could be making a trip to Provo to open the Playoff. If that does become true, expect fireworks from a physical standpoint. Also, LSU QB Sam Leavitt is not new for BYU. The former Arizona State QB would try to take two teams to the College Football Playoff. LSU and Lane Kiffin in LaVell Edwards Stadium for a playoff game would be great to see. Especially in the snow.

Brett McMurphy is one of the most reliable reporters in college football. While the projection seems a bit off, BYU in the CFP playing at reigning national champion Indiana in the first round seems unreal. The Hoosiers have TCU transfer QB Josh Hoover , who is starting to make his own path in Bloomington. If this happened, Curt Cignetti against Kalani Sitake would be great to see.

articles.title: FAW eyes more Wales games at Wrexham's Racecourse
articles.summary: FAW chief Noel Mooney wants Wrexham's Racecourse to host more internationals once the new Kop stand has been completed.
articles.body:
Chief executive Noel Mooney says the Football Association of Wales (FAW) wants Wrexham's Racecourse stadium to host more internationals once the new Kop stand has been completed.

The Racecourse – also known by its Welsh name Y Cae Ras - is the oldest international football ground still in use having staged Wales' first home game in 1877.

The ground has hosted 95 senior men's internationals in total, the most recent of which was a friendly against Gibraltar in 2023.

One completed, the Kop stand will be able to accommodate 7,500 fans and will help to take the overall stadium capacity past 18,000.

Speaking on BBC Radio Wales, Mooney said it was "brilliant to see the Cae Ras taking shape".

"We celebrated our 150th year this year up in Wrexham, where the association was formed," he added.

"We've played in Wrexham over the last few years, both the male and the female national teams have played there. They've really, really loved playing at Wrexham because it's the spiritual home.

"Our relationship with Wrexham is outstanding. We're talking to the club a lot about how we can use the stadium more but for sure, we'd love to play more internationals there."

Wrexham are looking to further develop the Racecourse with chief executive Michael Williamson stating that the ground's ideal capacity would be between 26,000 and 29,000.

Wales women have played games in Newport and Llanelli along with Cardiff City Stadium, which has become the home of Wales men's team.

There have also been suggestions that Craig Bellamy's side could play some fixtures at the 74,500 capacity Principality Stadium.

Mooney said a bigger capacity is essential if the FAW are to bring senior men's qualifiers back to Wrexham.

"We would love to play more matches in the Cae Ras, and as we can, we certainly will," Mooney added.

"The challenge for us is obviously the capacity. Cardiff City's is 32,000, 33,000 whereas Wrexham - even when it's complete - will be 17,000 or so.

"When we play Portugal, Denmark, Norway in the Nations League, we've sold a lot of campaign tickets. So the problem is we could have 18,000, 19,000 campaign tickets sold and therefore it makes it impossible for us to play a World Cup qualifier if you've that many season tickets sold."

He added: "How can you deny someone going to use their season ticket and so on?

"What we need Wrexham to be is a capacity where we can bring the competitive senior matches up there."

articles.title: Forlán debuta como seleccionador: "Hay que devolver a Uruguay al lugar que merece"
articles.standfirst: El exdelantero dirigirá ante Japón su primer partido como máximo responsable de La Celeste
articles.summary: El exdelantero dirigirá ante Japón su primer partido como máximo responsable de La Celeste
articles.body: Diego Forlán dirigirá hoy (12.00 de la mañana) ante Japón y en Japón, donde jugó en el Cerezo Osaka, su primer partido como nuevo seleccionador de La Celeste. En principio, estará al cargo en esta ventana y en la de noviembre. Y luego, dirigirá a la Sub 20 en el Sudamericano de la categoría en enero-febrero próximos. Será una Uruguay con muchos de los jugadores que acudieron al Mundial pasado, pero sin Fede Valverde, que se quedó en Madrid por el esguince de tobillo Grado 3 que se produjo en el derbi. Y sin Luis Suárez, que, tras conversar con Forlán, no regresará por ahora a La Celeste. Ayer, en su rueda de Prensa, Uruguay reivindicó su lugar y estaba convencido de su misión, que irá en teoría hasta que se produzcan elecciones en la AUF y nombren (o no) a un nuevo seleccionador. "Uruguay está obligado a ganar y hay que devolver a Uruguay al lugar que pertenece", dijo 'El Cacha'. Forlán seguirá la saga de su padre (leyenda como jugador de Uruguay, aunque también fue entrenador en el Sao Paulo brasileño) y seguirá el legado de su abuelo materno, Juan Carlos Corazzo, único seleccionador uruguayo que ganó dos Copas Américas (1959 y 1967, en la que dirigió a su yerno, Pablo Forlán, casado con su hija). Diego Forlán, recordemos, fue doble Bota de Oro con Villarreal y Atlético; fue campeón de América en 2011 con La Celeste; y Balón de Oro en Mundial 2010. Hoy se abre una nueva etapa en su vida.

articles.title: El hijo del mítico Roger Milla juega en Segunda con el filial del Celta
articles.standfirst: El histórico delantero que disputó tres Mundiales con Camerún, entre ellos el de España en 1982 (uno de los partidos en Balaídos), es el padre de Germain, futbolista del Celta Fortuna
articles.summary: El histórico delantero que disputó tres Mundiales con Camerún, entre ellos el de España en 1982 (uno de los partidos en Balaídos), es el padre de Germain, futbolista del Celta Fortuna
articles.body: "Antes no teníamos academias, teníamos sólo un entrenador. No había nada como esto”. A Roger le sorprendieron las instalaciones en las que iba a formarse como futbolista su hijo Germain, una vez cerrada en 2022, a través del convenio que se mantenía con el Fursan Hispania, club de Dubái fundado precisamente por Míchel Salgado, su incorporación a la cantera del Celta. Roger y Germain comparten el apellido Milla, lo que remite, en el caso del primero, al Mundial de 1982, 44 años han pasado, primero de los tres que, junto a los de Italia’90 y Estados Unidos’94, jugó con Camerún. Aquella selección dejó una huella imborrable en la cita de nuestro país, no perdiendo un solo partido, por más que cayera eliminada, en el grupo que compartía con Polonia, Perú e Italia. Precisamente el tercer y último duelo, frente a la selección transalpina, posterior campeona, se disputó en Vigo, en el estadio de Balaídos, con Milla asistiendo a M’Bida en la diana de los Leones Indomables. Roger, cuyo legado fue homenajeado por la propia FIFA en otro Mundial, el de Qatar, puede presumir sin duda de haber sido uno de los mejores futbolistas africanos de todos los tiempos, haciendo carrera sobre todo en el fútbol francés, tras pasar por Mónaco, Saint Etienne o Montpellier, y ganando además dos Copas de África con su combinado nacional. De tal palo, como suele suceder, tal astilla... Porque Germain, a sus 20 años, ya ha llegado al fútbol profesional después del ascenso a Segunda de un filial, el olívico, al que se había incorporado finalizada la campaña 24-25 y después de renovar contrato por cuatro temporadas. Suele desempeñarse por banda, con tendencia a ganar metros más allá de que la propia web del Celta lo presente como defensa. Y de momento ha participado en las seis jornadas disputadas en la Hypermotion, contribuyendo a un decimoquinto puesto que, con mucho por jugarse aún, mantiene a los de Fredi Álvarez alejados del peligro. Roger, mientras, contempla orgulloso la evolución de su hijo. ‘Voltarei’, dice la canción del Celta. Y volvieron. Los Milla volvieron.

articles.title: "La prioridad del Betis es satisfacer a su aficionado"
articles.standfirst: Emilio García Duarte, director de Negocio, participa del excelente momento deportivo y comercial que vive el club verdiblanco después de 15 años trabajando para la NBA
articles.summary: Emilio García Duarte, director de Negocio, participa del excelente momento deportivo y comercial que vive el club verdiblanco después de 15 años trabajando para la NBA
articles.body: Emilio García Duarte da la razón a Sergio Canales en eso de que uno nace de un equipo... pero también puede hacerse de otro. "Soy de Badajoz y del Badajoz, pero desde que estoy aquí el Betis me tiene loco". El director de Negocio llegó al club en abril de 2025... después de 15 años en la NBA. Eso que ha salido ganando su mujer, verdiblanca de toda la vida. Pregunta. Año y medio ya en el Betis... Respuesta. Es una experiencia estupenda. Había estado 15 en la NBA, los últimos 12 viviendo en Nueva York, y el cambio a una ciudad tan maravillosa como Sevilla es un regalo. Y luego también doblemente contento por cómo están marchando las cosas, por cómo está funcionando el equipo tanto a nivel deportivo como a nivel comercial. Pregunta. ¿Quién le fue a buscar? Respuesta. Es una historia un poco larga, pero curiosa. Yo tenía un amigo que trabajaba en la NBA y ahora tiene una empresa que se dedica al mundo del deporte, y esta persona tenía conocimiento de que el Real Betis buscaba candidato para las plazas de directores de Negocio y Marketing. Entonces ahí es cuando contacto con el club y empieza un proceso de entrevista que acaba con mi contratación. Unimos la oferta y la demanda bastante rápido, porque yo tenía ganas de volver a España y se trataba de una oportunidad que me atraía mucho. Pregunta. ¿Qué diferencias hay entre la NBA y LaLiga? Respuesta. Hay muchos cambios pero también hay similitudes, porque yo creo que LaLiga ha seguido un modelo muy parecido al de la NBA. De hecho muchas veces yo recibía visitas en nuestra oficina de Nueva York y sé que servíamos como referencia. Quizá la mayor diferencia esté en el plano comercial precisamente, porque la NBA es una organización que tiende a monetizar la relación con el aficionado de manera mucho más intensa, mientras que en fútbol y en LaLiga la prioridad es la satisfacción de ese aficionado, muchas veces por encima de exprimirlo. La NBA es una empresa que sabe muy bien quién es su aficionado, qué es lo que le gusta, cuáles son las cosas que consume y que, en función de todo eso, es capaz de sacar el mayor rédito económico de cada uno. De hecho hay una métrica que se monitorea mucho siempre, que es el valor económico vital. Es decir, cuánto dinero a lo largo del año se deja el aficionado en un equipo o en la Liga. Pregunta. Pero ahí queda un poco de lado el sentimiento de pertenencia... Respuesta. Totalmente de acuerdo. En el mundo del fútbol existe un componente pasional y de comunidad que en el ámbito de la NBA no está tan arraigado. Los equipos de baloncesto son marcas globales y las operan pensando no sólo en el aficionado local, sino también en ese aficionado global. Y muchas veces se pierde esa identidad y ese lazo con la comunidad. Eso aquí no pasa tanto. Una de las cosas que sí he intentado implementar dentro del Betis es tener un poco más esa visión internacional de la marca, pero por supuesto sin olvidarnos de que el centro de nuestra actividad está en el aficionado local. Pregunta. Una cosa es ser hincha y otra es ser cliente... Respuesta. Hay una palabra que se utiliza mucho en la NBA, que es fan, que a mí no me gusta tanto porque puede tener unas connotaciones negativas asociándolo con el fanático. En ese sentido las ligas americanas no distinguen, porque cualquier aficionado es un potencial cliente. Aquí los hinchas no tienen necesariamente que consumir productos de un equipo, pero sí consumen un contenido u otro tipo de productos que, aunque no son monetizables, también forman parte del ecosistema del Betis. Y es importantísimo conocer bien a tus aficionados y sobre todo manejar bien los datos e invertir en sistemas e infraestructuras. Ése es un camino que ya hemos iniciado, precisamente para saber qué les gusta, qué consumen, cuáles están dispuestos a comprar nuestros productos y cuáles no pero sin embargo siguen teniendo una relación con nosotros... Nosotros tenemos 99.000 socios actualmente. Algunos son socios con asiento y otros sin, pagando una pequeña membresía. Otro producto es el 'Soy Betico Digital', por el que no se paga absolutamente nada. Y eso nos ayuda a configurar una base de aficionados. Además un 40% de nuestros abonos son bonificados según categorías: socios infantiles, socios juveniles, personas mayores de 65 años, abonados con un grado de discapacidad igual o superior al 33%, abonados desempleados o con rentas que no superan los 16.500 euros brutos al año... Y por supuesto las cesiones de abono o las mejoras, que convierten el abono infantil en abono de adulto por un módico precio. Pregunta. ¿Y cómo es el aficionado del Betis? Respuesta. Me he dado cuenta de ese amor incondicional que hay por este equipo. Esa pasión que existe en el aficionado del Betis es algo imposible de ver en otras latitudes del mundo y menos en el deporte estadounidense. Yo lo calificaría como un aficionado muy leal, con un amor por los colores increíble y que se demuestra todos los días. Cualquier decisión o cualquier noticia, por pequeña o grande que sea, trasciende los límites de la ciudad y eso es maravilloso desde el punto de vista del negocio, pero sobre todo desde la creación de valor de marca que aporta. Pregunta. ¿Demasiados frentes abiertos en el club? Respuesta. Sí, sí, cada día más, pero eso es muy positivo. Creo y me gusta decir que el mismo equipo de Champions que hemos hecho para el terreno de juego es el que hemos hecho en las oficinas. Hay que agradecer a esta directiva que valore tanto el talento y la meritocracia. Y en ese sentido hemos incorporado personas de diferentes puntos de España y del extranjero, porque creemos que pueden aportar mucho valor y talento. Seguimos construyendo un equipo robusto que nos permita crecer no sólo a nivel deportivo, que también, sino a nivel comercial y a nivel de organización. Pregunta. La Cartuja es la casa actual del Betis, pero el Villamarín es su hogar. Respuesta. Yo creo que al final el Benito Villamarín es y será siempre la casa de los béticos, y además que con el nuevo estadio vamos a tener un potencial de seguir creciendo estupendo, pero la verdad es que en La Cartuja ahora mismo estamos también muy bien. Nos está dando nuevas posibilidades y tiene más aforo. De hecho somos los terceros con más asistencia, lo que demuestra el tirón y la base social tan importantes que tiene este equipo. El año pasado tuvimos casi un millón cien mil personas asistiendo a los partidos, prácticamente 200.000 más que la temporada anterior en el Villamarín. Además este estadio también nos ha permitido incrementar la oferta para los clientes Premium, porque tenemos 2.647 asientos Vip, con una ocupación de casi el 100% por partido. Eso demuestra el interés por tener experiencias diferentes para clientes diferentes, y hemos tenido que hacer una inversión importante para que esos nuevos espacios tuvieran la calidad que nosotros considerábamos. No nos hemos cambiado a una casa peor, sino a una también buena y más grande, pero siempre teniendo en mente que vamos a volver a la nuestra, que es donde mejor se está. Pregunta. ¿Trabajan con la vista ya en el retorno? Respuesta. El cambio nos va a servir también para testear y para aprender de cosas que se pueden hacer mejor y con las que cuando volvamos al Villamarín daremos mejor servicio a los aficionados. Y por supuesto que ya estamos teniendo en el horizonte esa vuelta, porque nos va a traer una proyección de ingreso sustancial que luego repetiremos en la plantilla y que ayudará a que el equipo compita mejor y a que en general la organización sea más competitiva en el día y día y esté preparada para los retos del siglo XXI. Pregunta. ¿El naming del nuevo estadio forma parte también del negocio? Respuesta. Es una parte muy importante, porque supone una fuente de ingresos. En ese sentido nos permitirá tener un patrocinador principal y el que golpea primero en este caso tiene ventaja. A todos se nos vienen a la cabeza estadios a los que se sigue llamando de una manera determinada aunque ya tengan otro patrocinador. Pregunta. ¿Cómo es la relación entre el despacho y el césped? Respuesta. Yo creo que es un círculo virtuoso, que todo está comunicado. Si a nivel financiero las cosas no van bien, evidentemente no se puede traspasar la plusvalía a la parte deportiva, no se pueden traer mejores jugadores y no se puede competir mejor. Y viceversa: si la parte deportiva no funciona bien, de alguna forma también impacta a la parte financiera. Por eso se hace hincapié en la importancia de tener equipos profesionales en ambas áreas. En todo eso hay una visión de liderazgo por parte de la presidencia y la directiva, que han sabido atraer talento a la organización y, una cosa también muy importante, han sabido darle autonomía. En ese sentido también reconozco que mi incorporación al Betis ha sido muy placentera porque me dejan libertad hacer cosas. Pregunta. ¿Cómo es su relación con esos dirigentes? Respuesta. Bueno, creo que son personas cercanas, muy profesionales, que han trasladado su visión empresarial al Betis. Yo comparo con lo que he visto en la NBA y honestamente hay muy pocas diferencias a nivel de gestión. El Betis no tiene metodología de pequeña empresa o de empresa familiar, pero eso no se consigue de la noche a la mañana. Tiene que haber una visión desde arriba que imponga el modelo de empresa que se quiere. Pregunta. ¿Cuáles serían las cifras que maneja el Betis de las que se siente más orgulloso? Respuesta. Lo más importante es que se ha producido un crecimiento a nivel económico y a nivel comercial constante y saludable. Hemos crecido en los últimos tres años a un ritmo de un 8% anual y hay que tener en cuenta que el tanto por ciento que supone la parte comercial en el total de ingresos es más relevante, a día de hoy el 40% aproximadamente, por lo que ya no tenemos una dependencia tan grande de la televisión o de las competiciones deportivas. En el ámbito del patrocinio estamos llegando a más acuerdos internacionales con diferentes marcas que tienen mucho interés en asociarse con el Betis, en la parte de 'hospitality' hemos crecido muchísimo con una oferta 'premium' cada vez de más calidad, en la parte de 'retail' cada día estamos vendiendo más equipaciones, en la parte de 'e-commerce', por ejemplo, el año pasado hicimos casi dos millones de euros sólo en venta de camisetas. Somos de los pocos equipos que gestionan sus tiendas propias , porque en la NBA, por ejemplo, eran modelos licenciados. Aquí tenemos autonomía para decir cuáles son las que queremos abrir, cuáles son las que funcionan, cuáles son las que no... En líneas generales creo que el club en todas esas líneas está funcionando muy bien, ahora tenemos que seguir creando valor y para ello estamos viendo nuevas fuentes de negocio, muy enfocados como decía antes en la parte tecnológica de conocer mejor a nuestros aficionados y de tomar decisiones a base de datos, no dejando nada al azar o a la intuición. Tenemos un departamento de innovación que se encarga precisamente de buscar nuevas oportunidades que puedan generar nuevos ingresos. Pregunta. El Betis es un club también posicionado por lo social... Respuesta. Sí, yo creo que al final todo ayuda para hacer marca. Un posicionamiento muy en la línea con los valores y la ideología de todo el club ha ayudado a potenciar esa imagen de un Betis agradable. De hecho somos el segundo equipo en la mayoría de las regiones, y eso viene de un trabajo previo, muy estudiado, por el que hemos decidido implicarnos en muchas causas sociales con el convencimiento de que eso va a hacer un mundo mejor. Ahora lo hemos hecho contra el acoso escolar, pero también con el medio ambiente a través de nuestro programa Forever Green. Yo creo que todas esas cosas ayudan a que el Betis sea percibido como un club amigo y a venderlo internacionalmente, porque se añade el hecho de que tenemos una ciudad magnífica como Sevilla. Siempre digo en broma que Cleveland es 'invendible', pero Sevilla... Pregunta. También cuenta con una plantilla comprometida... Respuesta. Totalmente. Además cuando los conoces personalmente te das cuenta del compromiso que tienen para las acciones sociales. Yo he visto por ejemplo a Bartra quedarse el último en una cena y ayudar a las personas de la limpieza para recoger toda la mesa. Son actos que te muestran realmente de qué están hechas las personas, y luego esos mismos valores se traducen perfectamente cuando les pides cualquier tipo de colaboración. Pregunta. ¿Qué supone la participación en Champions a nivel Negocio? Respuesta. Es un salto cualitativo, porque te da una exposición todavía mayor y te permite llegar a nuevas audiencias, con lo cual obviamente sirve de trampolín. Luego hay que hacer un trabajo importante para que esa proyección se traduzca en oportunidades y negocios, pero es verdad que la Champions te permite ser visible en mercados que para nosotros son muy importantes, como Brasil, como Irlanda ahora con Troy Parrott, como China... Pregunta. ¿Está siendo para tanto lo de Parrott? Respuesta. Sí, sí. Estamos viendo una actividad increíble. A pesar de ser una empresa grande, el Betis todavía mantiene la agilidad que te permite aprovechar esas oportunidades. Obviamente nosotros desde lo comercial no tenemos ninguna influencia en los fichajes, pero sí podemos subirnos al carro para aprovechar la importancia de fichar a Troy Parrott, un internacional con una llegada estupenda y que está generando que se disparen las ventas de camisetas, el contenido a través de las redes o las iniciativas que nos llegan desde su país. Es un auténtico 'boom'. Pregunta. ¿Qué desafíos se plantea a partir de ahora? Respuesta. Estoy enfocado en que mantengamos el crecimiento financiero y comercial, pero también en que tenga una base sustentable y rentable. Otro de los grandes retos es generar nuevas fuentes de ingreso que supongan un cambio diferencial para la organización, aunque en el mundo del deporte está casi todo inventado y hay que ser muy creativo. Expandir la marca y llegar a nuevas audiencias completarían los cuatro grandes objetivos actuales.

articles.summary: 'Al otro lado del espejo', por Alfredo Relaño
articles.body: Luis de La Fuente ha tapado el agujero en el lateral derecho (lesión de Porro y baja voluntaria de Llorente), con un desconocido para la gran mayoría de la afición, Iván Fresneda. Nacido en los alrededores de Madrid, náufrago de la cantera blanca, de la que saltó a las del Leganés y el Valladolid, en la capital castellana llegó a jugar. Allí es más fácil que le recuerden. Tuvo su momento de gloria por un marcaje a Vinicius cuando este andaba en mejores días que los actuales, pero en 2023, con 19 años, saltó al Sporting de Portugal, donde le perdimos la pista. De la Fuente le rescata ahora del olvido. El caso es parecido al del nuevo tercer portero. Ante la falta de Joan García ha elegido, por delante del clásico Remiro, al meta del Inter, Josep Martínez, del que sólo teníamos noticia previa por la casualidad de que hace muy poco que se enfrentó al Madrid, con la desdicha de regalar un gol y el mérito de salvar luego otros. Nacido en Alcira, pasó fugazmente por Las Palmas hasta buscarse la vida fuera, pasando por el Leipzig y el Genoa hasta instalarse en el Inter. No son casos raros, responden la dinámica que venimos viendo en la lógica del fútbol viajero e interconectado de este tiempo. Del mismísimo Olmo sólo tenían noticia los muy estudiosos del fútbol internacional cuando jugando en el Dinamo de Zagreb le llamó Luis Enrique en la Selección. Sorpresas de ese tipo fueron también en su momento los metas Raya y Robert Sánchez, horneados en la Premier, Grimaldo, pescado de la Bundesliga, el antes citado Porro, ese pacense forjado, como su sustituto, en el Sporting de Lisboa, y Huijsen, que nos vino del Bournemouth. Algunos tuvieron un paso fugaz por aquí, otros ni eso. Todos eran desconocidos para el macizo de la afición cuando se produjo la llamada. La salida al exterior les dio oportunidades, les endureció el carácter, y el equipo técnico de la Federación ha hecho bien su tarea de mirar por encima de las fronteras. España exporta futbolistas, y no sólo consagrados, como ahora Ferran Torres, sino también en etapa de formación.

articles.title: Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe lost their husbands - this is their story
articles.summary: Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe speak to the BBC's Simon Jack at the launch of a new suicide prevention toolkit.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide and information some readers may find distressing

Two women, united in grief, are meeting for the first time.

Debbie Beard lost her husband just over a year ago. Matt Beard, the former Liverpool Women manager, died in hospital on 20 September 2025. He is believed to have taken his own life, though an inquest is yet to conclude.

Amanda Thorpe's husband Graham, the former England and Surrey cricketer, took his own life in 2024. He had "spiralled into depression" after losing his job as a batting coach in 2022.

The two women, who had never met before, came together at an event launched by the Prince of Wales and the Royal Foundation to urge sport at every level to make suicide prevention part of its culture through a new nationwide toolkit.

There they spoke to the BBC's business editor Simon Jack , who was 17 when his father took his own life.

On Your Side , external is a set of resources available online that aims "to make suicide prevention as much a part of sport as warm-up, training and performance".

Amanda Thorpe has said previously she believes her husband would still be alive had he received more support from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) after leaving his coaching role. Following the inquest into his death, the ECB said it was "a profound tragedy" and added Thorpe's passing was a "stark reminder" of the challenges many face with mental health.

Matt Beard died a month after leaving his role as manager of Burnley Women. He had been in the post for only two months. When the inquest into his death was postponed indefinitely, Burnley said they were "aware of an ongoing legal process" and would "not be making any comment at this time".

Amanda: "Graham had been struggling for the previous year to 18 months during Covid. Graham didn't really like following rules and there were quite a few in Covid - like playing under bubble conditions. So he had been having some medication and therapy in his job. But then Graham lost his job and he didn't see it coming.

"He did pride himself with having been in the game his whole life. He just couldn't believe that he was blindsided by it.

"I think at least two other people were sacked at the same time, which does happen at the end of disastrous Ashes series.

"Also he was probably drinking too much and found the whole of the last trip in Covid very stressful. He then took a playful video at the end of the tour, when they had a few drinks with the opposition. One of the players sent it to two friends and someone unfortunately leaked it, so it was in the Sydney Morning Herald."

Simon: "Going for a few drinks with the opposition - you would think that that happens in sport all the time, but they lost?"

Amanda: "Yes. It's OK if you win but you're not allowed to have a drink if you lose. He was probably in shock. He couldn't believe it. And he was embarrassed and ashamed about this stupid video, which to me he blew way out of proportion. But he was in this tunnel where he thought he'd messed it all up. So he went into a quick and steep decline."

Simon: "During that period, what could have been done? You said that he was seeking some help. What might have made a difference, do you think?"

Amanda: "He was having therapy sessions. He had 10 sessions. There's obviously the confidentiality but I found out after he made a very serious attempt on his life, when he really hurt himself very badly, that he'd mentioned suicide. I didn't know about that at the time. Of course, I feel that if I'd known, things could have been different. And I did feel that he wasn't really getting better. It was difficult. I felt like maybe he did need more help - maybe residential but we didn't really know where to find that."

Simon: "Debbie, Matt also lost his job..."

Simon: "Were there any signs that he was struggling with mental health, and then was there a steep decline afterwards?"

Debbie: "I think there were changes in behaviour, looking back. Performance-wise the team weren't doing well so there was a lot of abuse on social media. He could never really speak his truth during media interviews of what was going on behind the scenes and he used to sound off to me at home.

"I've found out since that he had spoken to his brother quite a lot about his mental health. But whenever I would say to Matt 'how are things?', he'd be, 'I'm all right, I'm all right', because he always wanted the best for other people.

"He didn't want to concern me and the family that he was having these thoughts and that he was going through these different struggles.

"The sacking came out of the blue and there was a lot of speculation around that. He was starting to drink more than he would have done normally. In terms of his behaviour, I would say he was taking a lot of risks as well. So maybe that was the start of this with him."

Amanda : "Graham was known as a tough competitor. He was a very happy person and loved life, but it can happen to anyone. He wasn't thinking straight really because everything kind of became a vortex. And he just sort of lost the ability to be able to be grounded and think straight. Also you think you're thinking straight when you're not."

Simon: "One of the things about sport that's been discussed is that its reach is enormous. Coaches have a very intimate and closely proximate relationship with people. They can see what's going on with them - even at grassroots level. What would you encourage people to do if they see other people struggling, either in their family or in their community?"

Debbie: "It's a very difficult conversation. It's very hard. But if you're with these people day in, day out, you notice the changes in them. Matt was very intuitive with his players - he could sense things if they weren't playing right. He might have had a conversation with them just one-to-one, away from everyone else, and then make suggestions. There's an awful lot of emphasis on the physical side of someone's wellbeing, but not the mental side. That needs to be explored with people."

Simon: "It's a tough conversation to have, isn't it? Even with your nearest and dearest, let alone with someone on the team. I wonder whether Matt found it difficult when he had to sack players or drop them from the team.

Debbie: "He did. He used to come home and say: 'I've had a hard conversation today with such and such, I've had to let them go and there were tears.' And he'd say: 'I feel guilty.' He was the one who had to deliver the news. He felt tremendous guilt about letting people go."

Simon: "What did Graham's friends in the game come and say to you afterwards? You must have known them - you would have been part of that community."

Amanda: "They were really sad and really gutted. When he was really ill he was ashamed and he shut a lot of people out. So it was hard to get through to him. He would say: 'I've lost all my friends.' And I'm like: 'You haven't.' You know that's his brain. 'You haven't lost your friends at all,' I'd say. But that's how he felt. He felt very isolated."

Simon: "Did Graham have high highs and low lows? I mean, when he scored 100 against Australia or whatever? I just wonder whether he was a person of heightened emotions?"

Amanda: "He always used to say: 'Don't get too down about it... it might not be your day.' And I think if you're going to be like that, then when there are the highs you don't go overboard. He'd say it's his job but it is difficult with people scrutinising what you're doing and everything."

Simon: "What is it that you hope comes out of talking to us and what the Royal Foundation is doing?"

Debbie: "I think with the Royal Foundation, it is exposing the issue and people are going to be talking about it. But there needs to be the right support for when people need it - when they ask for that help.

"It's just making sure that toolkit is followed through and there are people that you can connect with and talk to.

"A connection with a therapist is a difficult one because it's someone you're going to be opening a box to. You want to let everything out but you need to trust that therapist. So it's making sure that there's a good connection there as well - that you feel comfortable talking about your innermost feelings."

Simon: "This is pretty raw for you. Why do you think it's important to talk to the world about this?"

Debbie: "For me and my children, we don't want another family to go through this. It is pretty raw and it's not just the grief, it's the practical side. You've lost a second income. I've still got to pay the same amount of rent, bills, etc. It is the practicality of it and you're juggling all the time - making sure the children are OK... still doing the school runs."

Simon: "You're obviously sad. Are you're angry? Determined?"

Amanda: "I'm angry at myself as well - the guilt you have. 'Why didn't I say that?' And you've got all these 'what ifs'. So all of that nonsense. And, yes - angry as well. 'Couldn't we just have done something?' But, you know, we fall. You know I'm his wife and I still didn't expect that to happen and I ask why he had to go through such a horrible thing. You wouldn't wish it on your worst enemy - and then there's the family as well - my daughters.

"My youngest went off to uni and then Emma went too. So it was just me and the geriatric dog. So it was quite hard."

Simon: "But it's a road you're both on and I think it's a road you've helped a lot of people with by talking to us."

Debbie: "We've got each other. We've met today and we are going to meet again."

Amanda: "Yes, be a force to be reckoned with! Isn't that what they say?"

Debbie: "Yeah, so I'll come down to you, you come up to me. We're part of this club that we never wanted to be in but we are going to make people listen to what we've got to say. We just want to make a change and help people and just highlight it - we never want anyone else to be in this position. We're going to go great guns aren't we?"

articles.title: Tony Pulis column: Why international break has come at worst time for De Zerbi & Spurs
articles.summary: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains the different factors that mean Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi needs time with his players to build a proper team.
articles.body:
Big spending always means big ambitions, but shelling out so much money on so many players the way Tottenham did this summer produces problems for any manager, and there is no quick fix.

If I was given a bundle of cash and asked to buy an outfit for a wedding, and I spent every penny of it on pink shoes, brown trousers, yellow shirt and orange tie, then I am sure you would all say that just doesn't work.

That is similar to what has happened at Spurs, where the board backed Roberto de Zerbi to the hilt with an outlay on new players of around £400m.

It was an almost unprecedented occurrence from a club that has always been renowned for being careful with investment in their team, and it sent expectations from many Spurs supporters through the roof.

The club had just avoided relegation two seasons running, finishing 17th twice in a row, but suddenly some fans were looking forward to a season competing for trophies and a top-four finish.

Their early results and performances have been disappointing, of course, but fans have to understand all the different factors that affect you when you are building a team - and it is ridiculous to suggest De Zerbi should be under pressure already, especially after he kept them up last season.

Finding a way for your club to win takes a manager in lots of different directions but they all involve time - on the grass or with social interaction with the players.

Not only has De Zerbi not been given that early time and opportunity, the majority of his players have now been taken away from him for another three weeks on international duty.

De Zerbi has many other issues to deal with, from Tottenham 's poor home form to their inability to recover from conceding the first goal in games.

But his biggest challenge right now will be to fit those players who have just arrived in with the ones already at the club, into a unit that plays as a team and produces results so that the money the club has spent is justified.

All of this will take time, and patience, and all the kinds of little detail that supporters never see.

In my day, we were given time to create a team, and a family. For today's managers, time seems more limited than ever.

We are only five games into the season but there are already some Spurs fans who seem to think De Zerbi is the worst manager in the world, even though he has proved elsewhere how good he is.

I like De Zerbi's passion, and his approach. That will count for nothing if Spurs don't eventually produce, but let's give him a proper chance.

De Zerbi is a very passionate, straight-talking and ambitious manager who demands total commitment and backing from his board.

He has definitely had that at Spurs, which has left people wondering why he has made such a slow start.

But, before the season started, I thought his biggest challenge with so many different types of players arriving would be to put players together that fit as a team, not as a group of individuals.

I've been in that situation myself, for example in my early days at Stoke, when I signed Gerry Taggart and Michael Duberry to play together, two centre-halves who were complete opposites in relation to how they dealt with space on the pitch.

Gerry always wanted to drop off deeper because he wasn't overly quick, whereas Michael was fast and didn't ever worry about leaving space behind him.

I couldn't make Gerry any quicker, so common sense locked in and I had to convince Michael that he would have to take a step away from his main strengths of pace and power and work along Gerry's lines instead.

We spent a great deal of time on the grass in training until we finally got both working in unison. Both were different, but they understood the importance of working together as a pair for the benefit of the team. Even so, it still took time for it to click.

For any manager trying to build a successful team by developing combinations like that, the main thing you need is time with your players.

It can happen where a lot of new players settle in quickly at the same time and the team starts well - like Sunderland last season, or Brighton pretty much every year when they have lost several key players - but the difference is that while those clubs might also have changed their manager, they have not changed their identity.

Whether it is Sunderland and Brighton , or Brentford and Bournemouth , they all have a set identity so that when they look for a player to fit in a certain position, he has to have certain strengths.

When you don't have that solid base behind you, knowing exactly what is needed for certain positions, then bringing 10 new signings and all in one window like Spurs have just done, is going to create many issues for the coach.

Each player has a different personality and needs different amount of time to settle in, not only to a new environment but also to adjust to the demands of a very single-minded and demanding coach like De Zerbi is.

This settling-in period would have been covered if all the players had had a pre-season together, to get up to speed with their team-mates and what De Zerbi is asking of them, with his front-foot style of play.

That did not happen, and then even after the season started, Spurs were still adding to their squad.

Finding out who understands importance of teamwork

Coaching a team to be a team takes time, patience and a sound idea of the strengths of all your players.

Even when you have got that, trying to knit every player together takes time, and that is still De Zerbi's issue now.

For starters, he was always playing catch-up. Because all of his players were not in place when the season began, he missed the opportunity to assess his squad and impose his own principles on his top group of players.

He is a coach at heart and will want to be out on the training pitch conducting a system of work for the team, in and out of possession, that he believes will bring success to the club. This international break means he cannot do that with all his players.

Another issue De Zerbi has is that he has only been in the job a few months and he is still getting to know the existing players, not just the new ones, on and off the grass.

On it, you need to find out who understands the importance of teamwork and who doesn't, to iron out shortcomings and and see what works and what doesn't.

An example of when you realise something doesn't work was my experience at a club who had just bought a right-back from a top Premier League team, for more than £1m which was big money at the time.

We were struggling at the bottom of the league when I came in and needed a direction on the pitch that would bring better results.

During the defensive work we were doing in training, the full-back kept picking up what were, in my opinion, poor positions while covering from the opposite side to where the ball was.

I must have stopped the session on at least four occasions to remonstrate with him and give my view, but in the end the lad told me that this is not what he believed was right.

I immediately replaced him with a young full-back from the reserves who had been playing for the opposition in the drill, who understood his role was for the team, and not for himself.

Getting to know your players' characters too

Getting things right off the pitch is so important too, and that involves getting to know what your players' characters are like, finding out what they are like as individuals, and understanding their lifestyles.

I had three South American players at West Brom who were fantastic lads but we still had to look after them.

I spoke to my assistant, David Kemp, about taking them and their families out for dinner, and by spending time with them and their children and their wives I believe we won a degree of respect and trust that we would never have had if we had not bothered to meet them all together as a family.

You have to realise that players from different cultures can be used to living a different lifestyle, and this can make a difference to how quickly or how well they fit in.

I had one player in the Premier League whose routine I just could not believe, yet he became such an integral part of keeping a struggling club up.

His 24 hours typically played out like this - training from 8.30am to 1pm, home and bed until 9 or 10pm and then up and out again for dinner and then a casino or whatever, until the early hours.

Then he would be up for training, and he would go again.

It took me a few weeks to get to the bottom of this but, once I confronted him, he was adamant that his routine suited his lifestyle. He certainly knew the best restaurants around town, but his performances were always of the highest quality on the pitch.

Did he heed my advice? I think he did, but he was such a great lad, top player and a great team member that he wasn't a problem anyway.

He had been a bit isolated from the rest of the squad at first, but it just took him some time to integrate.

Again, finding out about him as an individual and making personal contact with him, was important, and it was something I always saw as vital with all my players.

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

articles.title: Harry Kane eyes career as NFL kicker after football retirement
articles.summary: England’s captain and record goal scorer says a transition into American football could be on the cards.
articles.body:
England captain Harry Kane says he is considering a future as an American football kicker later in ⁠⁠his career, with the country’s leading goal scorer also eyeing a late move to Major League Soccer (MLS) in the United States.

Kane hinted at a late career in the National Football League (NFL) while speaking at England’s UEFA Nations League training camp on Wednesday.

Kane had previously expressed his interest in pursuing careers in golf and American football. ⁠⁠Now the 33-year-old is giving more serious thought to a future in the NFL, though he stressed any potential move to the US is still several years away.

“That is something ⁠⁠I will try and look at a bit more seriously,” Kane said. “It all depends on what happens in my career over the next five or six years. The NFL is a lot more realistic than the golf one, let’s put it that way.”

He is England’s leading goal scorer in international football with 85 in 121 appearances, 25 of which came from successful penalty conversions.

The Bayern Munich striker said his penalty-taking experience could give him a head start as an NFL kicker, though switching sports would require serious preparation.

He said, “I take penalties and it is a very similar pressure and technique … In terms of training, I would be closer to that more than any other sport.

“But, with all elite sports, when you watch it on TV, people make it look easy; you think it is possible, but that is ⁠⁠not always the case.

“If I was to do it, it is ⁠⁠something I would take seriously. I would take maybe six months to a year of trying to practise beforehand.”

Kane also suggested a move to MLS could provide a way to combine the two sports.

“Maybe if I am in ⁠⁠the MLS in the future or somewhere like that it might be a thing where you could connect the two maybe with ⁠⁠the seasons,” he said.

Some other football players have earlier ⁠⁠made the switch. Dallas Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey was a first-round MLS draft pick by Toronto FC in 2017 but never made an official appearance for the first team. Jake Bates also played college football before becoming a kicker ‌‌for the Detroit Lions.

Kane’s immediate future, however, remains in football, with talks over a new contract at Bundesliga champions Bayern progressing and an announcement expected soon.

“We’re in good talks,” Kane said. “There’s ‌‌still ‌‌some things that we need to iron out. I’m happy there. I think it won’t be too long before there’s some sort of announcement.”

articles.title: England vs Spain: Anthony Gordon backs Thomas Tuchel's 'DNA' comments about possession and calls on Three Lions to focus on their strengths
articles.summary: Thomas Tuchel said control with possession is not in the DNA of England players after World Cup loss; Anthony Gordon agreed, explaining inbuilt ability for Spanish players; winger calls on England to focus on own strengths; Follow England vs Spain on Sky Sports website and App on Saturday
articles.body:
Tuchel was criticised for England's defensive retreat after Gordon's goal gave them the lead against Argentina in the World Cup semi-finals, an approach which ultimately allowed their rivals to turn the match around in the final stages.

Tuchel responded by hitting out at the 'DNA' of English players. "I think ball possession plays a crucial role; it's maybe not in our DNA like it is in Spanish DNA or in Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball," he said.

Tuchel made those comments despite leaving some of England's most technical players - Cole Palmer, Phil Foden, Trent Alexander-Arnold - out of his World Cup squad, and not giving midfielder Kobbie Mainoo a minute of game time during the tournament.

However, speaking ahead of England's Nations League opener with world champions Spain, Gordon has backed his manager's view.

"England, as a nation, we don't have that strength, like the Spanish, where we control games like they do," said Gordon in a press conference. "It's not in us."

Gordon was speaking at St George's Park, a venue created to develop young English players in a technical style inspired by countries such as Spain, where former FA chief football officer Dan Ashworth outlined what became known as the 'England DNA' - an ironic backdrop given Tuchel's remarks.

Gordon, who now plays his club football in Spain for Barcelona, came through that system, starring in the country's successful youth teams, but said: "I'm not sure it's something that can be [taught].

"Playing in Spain, I can speak with an educated view on the way they keep the ball is different. It's much different than I've ever experienced playing in this country.

"I'm not sure we can ever get that but we can definitely get better, or maybe go the other way and really play to our strengths, which is play physical, play direct football, and on the counter-attack."

Speaking last week, Tuchel suggested England should perhaps "embrace the chaos" of that approach, and Gordon believes that could be the key lesson from the summer's World Cup disappointment.

"I think now that we've had that experience, probably the next time we're in that position, we'll go the other way," he said. "That scar doesn't have to be a negative one, because it might lead us to victory in the next tournaments."

'We're English and we have our own strengths'

Detailing the difference between Spanish and English players, Gordon said: "We, as English players, are educated the same way as the Spanish players. We know how to keep possession, but it's the decision-making of certain players in Spain which is just not a natural thing [for English players].

"I even look at some of the decisions they take on the ball sometimes and think, 'I'm not sure how you've seen that'. It's the way they're built.

"It's important for us that we can't keep looking at other countries and trying to be like them, because we're not them, we're English and we have our own strengths, which they don't have. So maybe we start playing to what we're good at."

Did iconic win in Mexico make England defensive?

Reflecting on the World Cup, Gordon also highlighted the impact of England's backs-to-the-wall, 10-man victory over Mexico at the Azteca, and how it subconsciously shaped their mentality for the subsequent matches against Norway and Argentina.

"The Mexico game was by far the best experience I've ever had in my life. But I think that probably set us up in a way," he said.

"The red card, it made us show a different side of us. We weren't so much the team that wanted to play anymore, we needed to really fight to get the victory, which we did. Then that probably became our MO a bit too much for the next two games, and ultimately didn't work for us in the semi-final."

Gordon, though, still backs the quality in the England squad - and is convinced they could have upset Spain in the final had they made it.

"I felt so confident," he said. "I felt like if we would have got to the final, I would have felt so confident playing Spain, that we would come out victorious, but we just didn't get there, so we'll never know."

It's not a World Cup final but England have the opportunity to show their level on Saturday at Wembley.

"If we can't be motivated to show what we can do at this level, then we're never going to be," said Gordon. "Spain are an incredible team.

"I spoke with the guys at Barca and said 'how would they have felt if we got to the final [instead of] Argentina?'

"They'd seen us as really competitive. It would have been a much more competitive game, because I felt Spain dominated the final. So maybe we can show that. We can show them how good we are.

"It won't replicate the final but playing against the best team in the world and winning and playing well, that'll do for now."

articles.title: Darren Caldeira: 'OCI players are a quick fix; grassroots must remain the priority'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Indian football enters a new era in the upcoming season with the Indian Super League (ISL) transitioning to a club-led model, placing greater
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Indian football enters a new era in the upcoming season with the Indian Super League (ISL) transitioning to a club-led model, placing greater responsibility on clubs to shape the league's commercial and sporting future. For Bengaluru FC, that means balancing ambition with sustainability while adapting to a fundamentally different operating landscape.In an exclusive conversation with TimesofIndia.com, Bengaluru FC's Director of Football Darren Caldeira speaks about the opportunities and challenges of the new ISL, the club's academy-driven recruitment strategy, the case for salary limits, the debate around Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) players, and why he believes long-term investment in youth — not quick fixes — will determine Indian football's future.EXCERPTSQ. The ISL is entering its first season under a club-led model. What do you make of it, and why did we reach such a stage?Darren Caldeira: I think it's a positive step in my opinion. If you look at it globally as well, it's not like this is a new phenomenon put together. It's not always that you have the federations running the leagues or somebody else coming in, like a commercial partner, like we had before (Football Sports Development Limited), running the league.So I think this club-led model, there's air of optimism from a lot of the conversations we are having, as well that probably this could be the right way forward. And while I say that, I don't want to sugarcoat things. There are still a lot of formalities that need to be closed.But I genuinely believe that we are heading in the right direction through a lot of these offline conversations, whether it's sponsorship or production, I will have to give credit to the FSDL as well in terms of a lot of the good work they've done. Because now that we are getting our hands dirty, actually being the ones that are having these conversations, whether it's broadcasters, whether it's sponsorship, you just realise there's so many things to cover. But then again, we've taken it up as a challenge.We're slowly onboarding a central team that comes in and we've already kind of had some soft integrations. But in my opinion, I think we are heading in the right direction.Q. From an organisational perspective, how do things change for clubs under this model?Caldeira: I think, more than anything, the whole commercial risk sits with the clubs, right? We are the ones having these hard conversations. Previously, it was FSDL speaking with production houses and broadcasters. We knew that we would be playing the league after paying X amount in terms of the franchise fee, and at the end of the year, there would be some sort of central revenue coming in. So that was a given.It was easier for clubs to plan as well because you knew what it would look like. Right now, there is that little bit of uncertainty that we talk about. You still don't know what the numbers would look like or what the Profit & Loss (P&L) would look like.We've got tentative numbers that we've put down, but a lot of owners are still a little more cautious, while also being excited about how we can take control of things, probably bring down costs in certain verticals and focus on the marketing of the league.So, more than anything, I would say the commercial risk is a big change.We haven't signed any domestic players this season. But there's a reason for that because we've got a very strong, robust youth academy that is churning out players year on year. We've had a couple of them make their debuts last season.Q. Has that uncertainty changed the way Bengaluru FC have approached transfers and squad building?Darren Caldeira: There are two things to that. We are a football club that has always been challenging for the ISL Shield or the title. We always want to win, right? But we are also mindful of the fact that the club economics have changed, and Indian football economics have changed.That said, we haven't signed any domestic players this season. But there's a reason for that because we've got a very strong, robust youth academy that is churning out players year on year. We've had a couple of them make their debuts last season.This time around, we didn't extend the contracts of four or five players. Some of them are leaders in the group as well. But we felt we had good replacements coming in from our B team to the first team.So the focus was on how we could probably get some good, solid foreign players in. Last season, we only had two foreigners in our squad, and we missed out on the title by three points.So you never know, if we had two or three more foreigners, we could have been a lot more competitive, probably taking it down to the wire. The focus was more on foreign players this time around because we knew we had the Indian contingent pretty much sorted.The idea was to get certain profiles that we felt would strengthen the team. There was a lot of work involved with Pep [Muñoz] and me to make sure we got the players who would enhance what we already had and would be essential to pushing towards the league Shield.We are a club that's very, very focused on that academy and we don't need to go and sign players from the outset. So even if tomorrow, we feel we've lost a quality player, maybe an Ashique (Kuruniyan) or maybe a Ryan (Williams) or someone. We know that we've got a replacement within the academy.Q. Is Bengaluru FC's academy-first approach the model Indian football should be following?Darren Caldeira: We've always been a football club (that is) big on the academy. You look at our first team right now, we've got more than half of the squad that have been part of our academy.And for us, it's a no-brainer. A lot of teams, when they had to strengthen their squads in the summer, had to reach out to other clubs, look at the free agents and things like that. And all we had to do was look right into our academy straight away to see who comes in.So for us, we're always looking to get those right players in because like I said, the economics of the league has changed as well. There's been this constant conversation about probably Indian players' salaries being inflated. I think that bubble has burst to a certain extent.But then again, we are a club that's very, very focused on that academy and we don't need to go and sign players from the outset. So even if tomorrow, we feel we've lost a quality player, maybe an Ashique (Kuruniyan) or maybe a Ryan (Williams) or someone. We know that we've got a replacement within the academy.Of course, we'll probably not be at that level and cannot hit the ground running, but we're ready to throw them in the deep end. I think Pep's also very big on age is not a factor. Nationality is not a factor to us. If you're good enough, you're old enough.Q. Should the ISL introduce salary caps?Darren Caldeira: 100 percent. We've had these conversations internally as well, and a lot of clubs have spoken about it. I think it's more about the clubs coming forward and saying, "Listen, this is the number, whatever that number is, and let's all stay within that."I think we've had salary caps in previous seasons as well. It's not like this is a new conversation we're having. I won't get into the details of whether people are following the salary caps or not, but there are always loopholes with any system.So I think the best way forward is for clubs to figure out how we fix this issue around salaries. The clubs are taking a step forward and coming together, saying, "Listen, we need to keep it within these numbers."We know that some of us have longer contracts with certain players, and you can't change those numbers now. But I think that conversation has already started, and we've already started making changes.While we're doing that, we're also figuring out a mechanism that can work because it's easier said than done. How do you have a bulletproof auditing system? It's not the MLS, where contracts are centralised and the league controls the contracts. Here, every club controls its own contracts.But, like I said, I think the clubs are making an effort, and that's a good sign.Q. Where do you stand on the idea of OCI players in the ISL?Darren Caldeira: So for me, when you talk about OCI players, I remember when that conversation started a couple of months ago, just like probably any other club, there were quite a few agents and the OCI players that reached out directly in terms of we are available, we are ready to come and we want to be part of the system.But I don't think it was well thought through. In my opinion, it was more about, there was a lot of public speaking about it, a lot of social media attention. But are these players wanting to come to Indian football for the right reasons? Will they actually come and spend those 2-3 years in Indian football, work on their paperwork and actually surrender their passport if they have to take that Indian passport?Something that I'd also like to mention is that sometimes when we think of OCI players and we think of foreign players, we already think of these players are better than our players, and that's not the case.Of course, there are a few who are playing at a certain level and will come in and change the whole dynamics of the Indian national team if that matters. But there are also a lot of players who are playing in Europe, but I wouldn't say are better than our Indian boys right now. So even if we have to go ahead with this, we need to be sure that we have a list of say 10-15 quality players from certain areas around the world, and these are the guys we want to get in.But more than anything, I think this is temporary. It's a quick fix. I think the focus should always be focussing on grassroots and the youth academy. And I think if all the stakeholders, everybody comes together, I think that should be the primary focus.Indian football as a whole, we can do everything we can at the club level and the league level, but it's really important that the national team does well. So every competition that they are participating in, whether it's your SAFF Cup or whether it's these friendlies that are coming now (against Panama, Brazil and Uruguay), good performances at the international level do help us because there are a lot of eyeballs.Q. What would success look like for the new ISL, for Bengaluru FC, and for Indian football?Darren Caldeira: I think, for starters, just going back to the home-and-away format and having a full-fledged season would be a good starting point. It's not a truncated format. We're going back to home-and-away, and we're having playoffs again. I really do wish we had another 30 or 60 days because we are having a lot of really good conversations, but it's so time-sensitive that you can't implement certain things that we want to.But whether it's your broadcasters, sponsorship, or an international partner wanting to come in, if we had that little bit of runway, I think it would be a lot better. But having a full-fledged season is one thing.It's just going back to what the ISL would look like and then gradually getting the right partners in, whether it's your sponsors. It could be as simple as your kit partners or your ball partners. But we're having a lot of encouraging conversations. While there is a lot of negativity surrounding Indian football, I won't deny that. There is still this air of optimism with the clubs kind of driving it and what Indian football looks like.At the club level, of course, it's Pep getting his first full season. I would love for him to be successful because he's a pretty solid coach. He brought a good bunch of players who have come in as well. And with our academy, it's about keeping the players coming through.And our soccer school, which I talk about as well, is more like a sort of business, and that does well as well. So overall, just for all of that, for the club to run smoothly, we move towards a sustainable model and we win trophies. And that's what I would see from a BFC level.And Indian football as a whole, we can do everything we can at the club level and the league level, but it's really important that the national team does well. So every competition that they are participating in, whether it's your SAFF Cup or whether it's these friendlies that are coming now (against Panama, Brazil and Uruguay), good performances at the international level do help us because there are a lot of eyeballs. People are watching from the outside, and the national team and the league go kind of hand in hand.
